rigs.name: Carolina rig
rigs.what: A slip-sinker rig: a heavy weight slides on the main line above a swivel, with a leader and hook below. The bait trails behind and moves naturally along the bottom.
rigs.use: Fishing soft plastics or live bait along the bottom, covering water in lakes or on grass flats.
need: Bullet or egg sinker (1/4 to 1 oz)
steps: Slide the sinker onto your main line, then the bead.
Tie the main line to one eye of the swivel.
Tie the leader to the other eye of the swivel.
Tie the hook to the end of the leader.
Add your bait, cast out and let it sink, then drag it slowly along the bottom.
rigs.tip: A longer leader gives the bait more room to move; shorten it if you keep missing bites.

rigs.name: Texas rig
rigs.what: A soft plastic worm on a hook with a bullet weight sliding on the line above it. The hook point is buried in the plastic so it does not snag.
rigs.use: Fishing in weeds, brush and around docks for bass.
need: Optional: small bead above the hook
steps: Slide the bullet sinker onto the line, point first toward the hook.
Tie the hook to the line.
Push the hook point into the nose of the worm and out the side, then slide it up over the bend.
Turn the hook and push the point back into the worm so it lies flat and weedless.
Cast near cover, let it fall, then lift and drop it slowly.
rigs.tip: Set the hook firmly when you feel weight or the line moves; the buried point needs a hard pull to come through the plastic.

rigs.name: Drop-shot rig
rigs.what: A hook tied on the line with a weight hanging below it, so the bait floats above the bottom at a set height.
rigs.use: Fish that sit just above the bottom in clear water or deeper spots, especially bass.
steps: Tie the hook to the line with a Palomar, leaving a tail of line 12 to 24 inches long, with the hook point up.
Tie or clip the weight to the end of that tail.
Hook the soft plastic through the nose.
Lower the rig until the weight touches the bottom.
Keep the line tight and gently shake the rod tip so the bait quivers in place.
rigs.tip: Change the distance between hook and weight to match how high above the bottom the fish are sitting.

rigs.name: Fish-finder rig
rigs.what: A bottom rig where the sinker slides on the main line, so a fish can pick up the bait and feel almost no weight.
rigs.use: Fishing bait on the bottom from a pier, bridge, beach or boat, especially for drum, redfish and snapper.
need: Sliding sinker (egg, pyramid or bank, enough to hold bottom)
steps: Slide the sinker onto the main line, then a bead.
Tie the main line to the swivel.
Tie the leader to the other end of the swivel.
Tie the circle hook to the end of the leader.
Bait it, cast out, and let the weight hold the bottom. Keep a little slack and let the fish take the bait before you reel.
rigs.tip: With a circle hook, do not jerk to set it: just reel steadily until the rod bends.

rigs.name: Pompano rig
rigs.what: A bottom rig with two short droppers, each with a small hook and often a bright bead, above a weight.
rigs.use: Surf fishing for pompano, whiting and other beach fish.
need: Pompano rig (ready-made or tied with leader line and 2 small hooks)
steps: Tie the main line to the top loop of the rig.
Clip or tie the sinker to the bottom of the rig.
Put a small piece of sand flea or shrimp on each hook.
Cast just past the breaking waves.
Keep the line fairly tight and watch for taps, then reel in steadily.
rigs.tip: Check the rig after every cast; the small hooks and beads tangle easily.

rigs.name: Knocker rig
rigs.what: A weight that sits right against the hook, with no leader. The sinker is 'knocked' down onto the eye of the hook.
rigs.use: Fishing right beside rocks, pilings, reefs and wrecks for snapper and grouper, where you want the bait kept near structure.
steps: Slide the egg sinker onto the main line.
Tie the hook directly to the line so the sinker rests on the hook eye.
Add the bait.
Lower it straight down beside the structure.
Keep the line tight and be ready to pull the fish away from the structure as soon as it bites.
rigs.tip: Use a heavy enough line: fish near structure will cut weak line quickly.

rigs.name: Free-line live bait rig
rigs.what: A live bait on a hook and leader with no weight, so it swims naturally.
rigs.use: Inshore fish such as snook, redfish and trout, around docks, mangroves and bridges.
need: Hook (circle hook is a good choice)
Live bait such as shrimp, pilchard or pinfish
steps: Tie the leader to your main line with an Albright or double uni.
Tie the hook to the end of the leader.
Hook the bait through the nose or just under the back fin.
Cast softly beside cover or let the bait swim out on the tide.
Let the line run out slowly. When a fish takes the bait, let it run for a moment, then reel.
rigs.tip: A light touch matters: a gentle cast keeps the bait lively.

rigs.name: Popping cork rig
rigs.what: A cork or float on the line above a leader and a live bait or lure. A pop of the rod makes a splash and a noise that calls fish in.
rigs.use: Fishing live shrimp or soft plastics over grass flats and near cover for trout and redfish.
steps: Thread the line through the cork and set the cork to the depth you want.
Tie the leader to the line below the cork.
Tie the hook or jig to the end of the leader.
Bait it and cast.
Pop the rod tip every few seconds, then pause so the bait sits still. Set the hook when the cork goes under.
rigs.tip: Set the cork to just above the grass so the bait hangs where the fish look.
